findings.claim: Algorithmic management is already a mainstream management infrastructure in the surveyed economies, but its broad definition includes systems that are not necessarily AI.
limits: Survey scope and broad tool definition are retained.

findings.claim: The management surface already includes worker speed, communication tone, fatigue, sanctions, targets, and leaderboards, creating a ready path from observation to adverse exertion.
limits: Capability and use-case taxonomy do not prove named deployment or abuse.

findings.claim: Electronic monitoring cannot be presumed to improve performance merely because it increases managerial visibility; the strongest aggregate review recovered no performance benefit and higher stress.
limits: Heterogeneous aggregate evidence is not a ban on all monitoring.

findings.claim: The acceleration risk is organizational: tools reduce latency and expand denominator coverage, allowing weak classification to reach more workers before context, support, or dissent can intervene.
limits: No universal purge or intent finding is made.

observations.claim: The OECD taxonomy includes algorithmic allocation of schedules, activities and clients; task instructions; monitoring of completion, time, speed, conversation content or tone, location, fatigue and safety; and evaluation through targets, rewards, sanctions and leaderboards.

In the OECD employer survey, 90% of US firms and an average 79% of firms in the surveyed European countries reported at least one instruction, monitoring or evaluation tool under the broad definition.
limits: Manager-reported firm adoption; not worker-level exposure or consequence.

observations.claim: Across surveyed countries, tools to sanction poor performance were reported less often than tools to reward performance, but sanctioning remained an explicit algorithmic-management use case.
limits: Adoption rate does not establish decision quality.

observations.claim: A meta-analysis of 94 independent samples and 23,461 workers found no evidence that electronic performance monitoring improved performance and found an association with increased stress.
A second meta-analysis of 70 samples found small decreases in job satisfaction and small increases in stress, with targets and feedback capable of exacerbating negative effects.
limits: Small aggregate effects; no case causation.

observations.claim: EU-OSHA reports increased monitoring, micromanagement, work intensity, pressure, reduced autonomy and privacy as worker concerns and identifies participation and transparency as mitigating factors.

title: Scale, managerial-function automation, and adverse-action latency
